newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy forecast shows EMU doubts, markets unworried.
newsitem.headline: Italy forecast shows EMU doubts, markets unworried.

text.p: The European Commission clearly has reservations about Italy reaching the financial goals needed to join Europe's single currency, but financial markets shrugged off the Commission's doubts, economists said on Wednesday.

The EU Commission forecast Italy's budget deficit to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) ratio at 3.2 percent for 1997 and then ballooning out to 3.9 percent in 1998, before taking into account Italy's 1998 financial budget.

A three percent deficit to GDP ratio is one of the financial criteria in the 1992 Maastricht Treaty for European nations wishing to join in Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). The Commission report said only Italy and Greece were scheduled to miss the target for 1997.
"The fact that Italy is above the three percent level suggests that the Commission has reservations about Italy's fiscal performance," said economist Ken Wattret at Paribas.
But financial markets took the forecast, which was reported last week in a newspaper here, in their stride and the lira, domestic bonds and the stock market showed little reaction.

The lira was largely steady around 995 to the mark while domestic BTP bonds held in positive territory although showing reduced gains and the Milan's stock market MIB30 index of Italy's top 30 stocks was up 0.48 percent at 18,346 by 1300 GMT.
Economists said that the diplomatic pressure to push down Italy's deficit/GDP forecast figure for 1997 had clearly failed, and that only emphasised the Commission's doubts over Italy.

Rome daily La Repubblica said earlier on Wednesday that the Commission was set to forecast the deficit/GDP ratio at 3.1 percent for 1997, which economists said would have been too close to argue that Italy should be excluded.

In the forecast, the Commission added that Italy's deficit/GDP ratio in 1997 may be 3.0 percent "if the (budgetary) measures already taken have full effectiveness and, if necessary, additional measures are introduced."

"It is a signal at the European level that Italy is rather weak and that other countries are unwilling to recognise the latest budget measures," said Lorenzo Codogno chief economist at Bank of America in Milan.
Alex Garrard, European economist at UBS in London, said, "This confirms that the Commission will look for further measures to trim these forecasts."

Economists said that the message to Italy from the Commission appears to be not to water down its 1997 15.5 trillion lire cutting mini-budget while its 1998 financial budget must be tighter than planned.

Italy's budget undersecretary Giorgio Macciotta added later that Italy was still in condition to reach the key deficit goal for EMU, and added that the government plans to draw up a 1998 budget of some 20 trillion lire ($11.7 billion) to meet the three percent deficit to GDP goal required for EMU.
